title: Morning Edition
dek: Brazil and Serbia vote; a humanitarian pause is planned in Ukraine; Nigeria's campaign begins; and what a parenthesis can reveal.

lead_story.headline: Brazil votes in a presidential runoff too close for polls to call
lead_story.summary: More than 158 million Brazilians are eligible to choose between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro on October 25. Datafolha's final October 23–24 survey gave Bolsonaro 51% and Lula 49% of valid votes, within a two-point margin of error. Voting has not yet concluded.
lead_story.why_it_matters: The outcome will determine the political direction of Latin America's largest country. In a close race, turnout and the actual count matter far more than a two-point polling lead.

items.headline: Serbia elects a parliament after two years of student-led protests
items.summary: Serbia's October 25 snap election chooses 250 lawmakers. A student-backed movement challenges the ruling Serbian Progressive Party after demonstrations that began with the 2024 Novi Sad railway-station canopy collapse. Polls disagree about the likely winner, and government formation will depend on seats, not just first place.
items.why_it_matters: The vote tests whether a sustained anti-corruption protest movement can convert public mobilization into parliamentary power—and whether voters regard the election process as credible.

items.headline: Ukraine and Russia agree on a limited humanitarian pause for Oleshky
items.summary: Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Ukrainian and Russian negotiators agreed that a local ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson would begin October 27. The proposed operation would clear routes, deliver supplies and permit voluntary evacuations. It has not yet begun.
items.why_it_matters: For civilians cut off from basic services, a narrow humanitarian corridor could matter immediately; it does not resolve territorial claims, guarantee safe passage or constitute a wider peace settlement.

items.headline: Nigeria's Tinubu opens re-election campaign amid a cost-of-living squeeze
items.summary: President Bola Tinubu formally launched the ruling APC's 2027 election campaign in Kaduna on October 24, defending his record and blaming opponents for hunger and poverty. His government's fuel and currency reforms have improved some macroeconomic indicators while imposing steep costs on households.
items.why_it_matters: Nigeria's campaign will test whether voters credit long-run fiscal reforms when everyday food, fuel and security concerns remain acute.

items.headline: Recent miss: French demonstrations draw hundreds of thousands, with disputed counts
items.summary: On October 24, protesters across France demanded relief on living costs and stronger public services. The Interior Ministry counted about 410,000 participants; the CGT union reported more than 800,000. Many marches were peaceful, but clashes and arrests followed in several cities.
items.why_it_matters: The different crowd estimates should be attributed rather than averaged. The protests reflect a wider conflict over public spending, education and who bears economic adjustment.

items.headline: Older catch-up: a satellite begins measuring the faint light of photosynthesis
items.summary: The European Space Agency launched FLEX and Sentinel-3C on September 15. FLEX is designed to measure the weak fluorescence emitted by plants during photosynthesis; Sentinel-3C extends monitoring of oceans, land and ice. The launch and initial contact succeeded, but routine scientific results are still ahead.
items.why_it_matters: The mission could eventually help researchers observe vegetation stress and productivity at large scales; an operational promise is not yet a demonstrated scientific finding.

items.headline: A new assessment puts nearly half of reef-building corals at elevated extinction risk
items.summary: A peer-reviewed reassessment of 892 reef-building coral species finds that nearly half face elevated relative extinction risk. Researchers used coral-cover trends and projected severe bleaching as proxies where species-level population data were missing.
items.why_it_matters: The result strengthens the case for treating reef loss as a biodiversity problem as well as a coastal and economic one. Its modeled classifications must not be confused with direct counts of every species' population.

items.headline: Auckland's Sandringham prepares a street festival around its many food traditions
items.summary: Sandringham Village in Auckland is preparing an October 31 street festival with neighborhood restaurants, cultural performances, school groups, music and family activities. A local reporter spoke with the event manager about the district's changing identity and preparations; the festival has not yet taken place.
items.why_it_matters: An ordinary neighborhood gathering can reveal a place through the people who cook, perform, shop and meet there, without needing a national news peg.

items.headline: The self may be something we do together, not something we own alone
items.summary: In an essay on Japanese philosopher Watsuji Tetsurō, Takeshi Morisato explains ningen as a relational account of being human: identity is shaped through relationships, language, place and an ongoing movement between individuality and community.
items.why_it_matters: The argument offers a serious alternative to treating the person as an isolated decision-maker, while raising questions about freedom, dissent and the pressure of social roles.

worth_your_time.headline: A parenthesis can reveal how a Renaissance writer thinks
worth_your_time.summary: Punctuation historian Florence Hazrat traces Philip Sidney's extravagant use of parentheses in his prose and letters. Brackets become more than pauses: they can protect vulnerable admissions, introduce digressions and stage the movement of a thought.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: A close reading of a small typographical mark opens an unexpectedly rich view of literary style, emotion and the history of how people learned to put thinking on a page.
worth_your_time.source: The Public Domain Review — Florence Hazrat

notes_for_next_edition: Report Brazilian and Serbian results only after official counts; avoid projecting from surveys.
Check whether the Oleshky corridor actually opens on October 27 and whether aid operators verify deliveries.
Follow up on France's November 5 mobilization without repeating today's protest card.
